reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A complication of gastric surgery (partial gastrectomy, pyloroplasty, vagotomy) and increasingly of bariatric procedures such as sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass, caused by loss of normal pyloric regulation of gastric emptying.

Early dumping occurs within about 15 to 30 minutes of eating and comprises both gastrointestinal (cramping, borborygmi, diarrhoea, bloating) and vasomotor (flushing, palpitations, tachycardia, light-headedness, need to lie down) features.
Late dumping occurs one to three hours after a meal and reflects reactive (postprandial) hypoglycaemia, presenting with sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion and palpitations.
A carbohydrate-rich meal, particularly rapidly absorbed simple sugars, is the classic trigger for both phases.
The modified Sigstad score and an oral glucose challenge with serial glucose and haematocrit measurement help confirm the diagnosis when it is uncertain.
First-line management is dietary: small frequent meals, restriction of simple sugars, separation of solids from liquids, and increased soluble fibre or viscosity-modifying agents to slow emptying.

Somatostatin analogues are the principal pharmacological option for refractory symptoms, slowing gastric emptying and blunting the vasomotor and hormonal responses; acarbose helps specifically with late dumping.
Surgical revision or feeding-tube strategies are reserved for severe, refractory cases after dietary and medical measures have failed.
reference.pathophysiology: Dumping syndrome arises when ablation or bypass of the pylorus allows rapid, unregulated delivery of hyperosmolar gastric contents into the small intestine. In early dumping, the hyperosmolar load draws fluid from the intravascular compartment into the bowel lumen, causing luminal distension, increased motility and a fall in plasma volume; this, combined with release of vasoactive and incretin gut hormones, produces the gastrointestinal and vasomotor symptoms. In late dumping, rapid absorption of carbohydrate provokes an exaggerated incretin (notably GLP-1) and insulin response; the insulin overshoot outlasts the transient hyperglycaemia and precipitates reactive hypoglycaemia one to three hours after the meal. The two mechanisms frequently coexist in the same patient.
additionalDifferentials: insulinoma and other causes of endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia
afferent or efferent loop syndrome after gastric surgery
bile-acid or bacterial-overgrowth diarrhoea following surgery
carcinoid syndrome and other neuroendocrine tumours causing flushing
anxiety or panic disorder with autonomic symptoms
additionalInvestigations: oral glucose challenge with serial glucose and haematocrit measurement
gastric emptying scintigraphy to confirm rapid emptying
continuous glucose monitoring to capture late postprandial hypoglycaemia
modified Sigstad scoring and structured symptom questionnaires
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or contrast study to assess post-surgical anatomy
72-hour fast or supervised testing where insulinoma is suspected
tests for bacterial overgrowth or bile-acid malabsorption when diarrhoea predominates
redFlags: recurrent severe hypoglycaemia causing loss of consciousness, seizures or falls
significant unintentional weight loss or malnutrition
hypoglycaemic symptoms occurring in the fasting state (pointing away from dumping toward insulinoma)
dehydration or syncope from severe vasomotor episodes
features suggesting mechanical complications such as afferent loop obstruction
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with dietary modification, and symptoms often attenuate over months to a few years as the intestine adapts; a minority have persistent, disabling symptoms requiring somatostatin analogues or surgical revision. Late dumping with recurrent hypoglycaemia can be dangerous and warrants prompt, structured management.
pitfalls: Confusing late dumping hypoglycaemia (postprandial) with fasting hypoglycaemia of insulinoma, leading to unnecessary or misdirected investigation.
Prescribing rapidly absorbed sugars to treat hypoglycaemic episodes, which perpetuates the cycle rather than resolving it.
Overlooking dumping in bariatric surgery patients, in whom it is now a common but under-recognised cause of postprandial symptoms.
Escalating to surgery before an adequate trial of dietary measures and somatostatin analogues.
Attributing vasomotor symptoms solely to anxiety and missing the temporal relationship to meals.
